## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## DEVONthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

1	---
2	status:
3	  - InProgress
4	priority: normal
5	dateCreated: 2026-07-05T19:48:25-04:00
6	dateModified: 2026-07-07T14:07:27.654-04:00
7	ContentType: Blog
8	tags:
9	  - task
10	---
11	Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.
12	
13	The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports." I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove. Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 
14	
15	Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive, doesn’t make it so.
16	
17	## Sectors
18	The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why those sectors? Based on what evidence.
19	
20	1. Health - improve Health Outcomes with AI? Where would we use AI and what evidence is there to support that it helps?
21	2. Energy and Natural Resources: AI used to optimize extraction and accelerate clean energy transformation? How
22	3. Transportation ...
23	
24	There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy is too vague to be useful here.
25	
26	## Healthcare
27	I will focus on the health sector. In Ontario, we constantly hear stories of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.
28	
29	Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 
30	
31	Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
32	- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
33	- Why are hospital beds so full?
34	
35	### Hospital beds
36	- Low population to hospital bed ratio
37	- Waiting lists for long term care
38	- Staffing shortages
39	
40	### Emergency Room Volume
41	- Lack of family doctor
42	- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
43	- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
44	- Seasonal flu et al
45	
46	None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 
47	
48	One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[1] to:
49	- Emergency Department volume
50	- Bed allocations and assignments
51	- Room cleaning
52	- Critical care capacity
53	- Surgical scheduling
54	- Discharge planning
55	
56	Reading the promotional PDF from GE the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.
57	
58	GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that they there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.
59	
60	AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. In this context, using an AI to find patterns and help make short term predictions seems very useful. GenAI is good at finding patterns.
61	
62	The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.
63	
64	AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, GenAI is just a tool in this picture.
65	
66	### Family Doctors and GenAI
67	Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 
68	
69	One of the challenges that they face, after a day of seeing patients they need to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.
70	
71	Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIPs payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.
72	
73	Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the names of problems and medications. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors.
74	
75	GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.
76	
77	Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.
78	
79	## Not a Magic Wand
80	GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be a very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.
81	
82	Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look a bigger than just an emergency room. In short look, it would seem we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 
83	
84	The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problems, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.
85	
86	https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/
87	https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all
88	https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/
89	https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports." I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove. Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive, doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why those sectors? Based on what evidence.

1. Health - improve Health Outcomes with AI? Where would we use AI and what evidence is there to support that it helps?
2. Energy and Natural Resources: AI used to optimize extraction and accelerate clean energy transformation? How
3. Transportation ...

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy is too vague to be useful here.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector. In Ontario, we constantly hear stories of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay

Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention{~~[1]~>[^3]~~} to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE{++[^4]++} the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that they there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. In this context, using an AI to find patterns and help make short term predictions seems very useful. GenAI is good at finding patterns.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, GenAI is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

One of the challenges that they face, after a day of seeing patients they need to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that {~~OHIPs~>OHIP~~} payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the {~~names of problems~>diagnoses~~} and medications. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors.

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be a very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look a bigger than just an emergency room. In short look, it would seem we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problems, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

The full source remains at `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/LLM-Related/marketingskills` if more skills are wanted later.

311	The skills have been re-pointed from their upstream default (`.agents/product-marketing.md`) to **`APR/brand-voice.md`** — the canonical APR product-marketing context, drawn from `strategic-business-overview.md` and the three voice skills. 313	### Copy Editing
314	**Purpose:** Edit, review, or refresh existing marketing copy through a seven-sweep framework (Clarity, Voice & Tone, So What, Prove It, Specificity, Heightened Emotion, Zero Risk) with optional expert-panel scoring for high-stakes pages. 323	**File:** `Skills/Marketing/marketing-psychology/SKILL.md`

336	**File:** `Skills/Marketing/launch/SKILL.md`

339	### StoryBrand Messaging

Output is suggestion-only and hybrid: the SB7 scorecard, diagnostic checks, and hero-violation flags stay in chat, while the 2-3 alternative phrasings for the weakest sections drop inline as CriticMarkup when the asset is a Markdown file (see criticmarkup-editing). Every alternative shows the stock StoryBrand version alongside an APR-voice-adjusted version (Mark chose this side-by-side mode). Does not propose alternatives to the canonical one-liner. Italicised passages in drafts are treated as Mark's author notes, not buyer copy. Distilled from the StoryBrand book; sits beside Marketing/copy-editing rather than replacing it (StoryBrand handles page-level narrative bones, copy-editing handles sentence-level tightening).
341	**Triggers:** "StoryBrand review," "SB7 review," "customer-as-hero check," "is this customer-focused," "is my sales page customer-focused," "review my sales page through StoryBrand," "review my nurture sequence," "review this opt-in," "brand script"
342	**File:** `Skills/storybrand-messaging/SKILL.md`
343	**References:** `references/brand-script.md`, `references/email-sequences.md`, `references/sales-conversations.md`, `references/multi-channel-consistency.md`, `references/one-liners.md`, `references/website-wireframe.md`
344	**Dependencies:** `APR/brand-voice.md` (mandatory pre-read for voice filter), `Skills/criticmarkup-editing.md` (inline delivery format), `APR/strategic-business-overview.md` (optional, for positioning context)
345	
346	---
347	
348	## Adding New Skills
349	
350	When you build a new skill:
351	1. Create the skill file in the `Skills/` folder
352	2. Add an entry to this index with triggers, purpose, and dependencies
353	3. Add the triggers to the Quick Trigger Reference table at the top
354	
355	The index is a living document. Update it every time you add, change, or remove a skill.
356	
357	---
358	
359	*Started with the Robot Assistant Field Guide Starter Kit. Customized in Video 5 via the assembler.*

16	# CriticMarkup Editing
17	
18	When Mark asks for feedback on writing that lives in a Markdown file, deliver it as inline

34	  file in place is correct and expected -- do NOT write to a `-reviewed.md` copy, because

37	## The Five Markup Types
38	
39	| Type | Syntax | Use for |
40	|---|---|---|
41	| **Comment** | `{>>Claude: your note<<}` | The default. Any feedback that needs explanation -- a "why," a question, a structural observation, a voice slip. Always prefix with `Claude:`. |
42	| **Addition** | `{++text to insert++}` | Propose inserting words/sentences. |
43	| **Deletion** | `{--text to remove--}` | Propose cutting words/sentences. |
44	| **Substitution** | `{~~old text~>new text~~}` | Propose replacing a specific span. The cleanest form for a concrete reword. |

# CriticMarkup Editing

format and the protocol.

| **Substitution** | `{~~old text~>new text~~}` | Propose replacing a specific span. The cleanest form for a concrete reword. |

content.text:
I've read the rubric and delivery format. This is a suggestion-only voice/logic critique, delivered as CriticMarkup. Per your review style I'll lead with the overview, then go section by section rather than dumping it all.

## Overview

The draft is close in voice and structure. The healthcare deep-dive is the strong core and reads very much like you: systems-thinking framing, concrete Ontario detail, the "assuming the AI makes no mistakes (unwise assumption)" move. Three things are worth real attention before it ships:

- **One content soft spot that undercuts your own thesis**: the line "GenAI is good at finding patterns" likely mislabels what the Humber/GE command centre actually runs (predictive analytics / classical ML, not GenAI). More on that when we get there.
- **The Sectors section is unfinished**: Transportation trails off mid-thought, and the section reads like margin notes rather than finished prose.
- **A cluster of typos/broken sentences in the closing** ("Not a Magic Wand") that need a cleanup pass.

Nothing here is a structural teardown. It's a strong draft with a few real holes.

Before I start writing marks into the file: do you want me to **drop the CriticMarkup inline as we go, section by section**, or **talk through all sections in chat first and mark up at the end**? Either way, here's the first chunk.

## Section 1: Opening + Sectors

**Opening (lines 11-15) - mostly on voice.**

- "I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove" (line 13). Good instinct, but you drop the reference without connecting it. A reader who doesn't know the film won't see why the 12%-to-60% adoption target is a manufactured gap. One clause tying it back would land it. Logic gap, not a voice issue.
- "Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive, doesn't make it so" (line 15). Comma before "doesn't" splits the subject from its verb. Minor rhythm snag.

**Sectors (lines 17-24) - reads unfinished.**

- Line 22: "Transportation ..." trails off. This is a draft hole, not prose.
- Line 18 "why those sectors? Based on what evidence." and the list items ending in bare questions read like notes to yourself rather than finished argument. Right now this section makes a promise ("the strategy is too vague") but shows less rigour than your healthcare section that follows. Either build it out to one tight example or compress it into a couple of sentences and get to Healthcare faster.
- The closing line (24) "The strategy is too vague to be useful here" is the payoff and it works.

Want me to continue to Section 2 (Healthcare + Humber River, where the GenAI/analytics content issue lives)?

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove. Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive, doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why those sectors? Based on what evidence.

1. Health - improve Health Outcomes with AI? Where would we use AI and what evidence is there to support that it helps?
2. Energy and Natural Resources: AI used to optimize extraction and accelerate clean energy transformation? How
3. Transportation ...

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy is too vague to be useful here.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector. In Ontario, we constantly hear stories of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that they there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. In this context, using an AI to find patterns and help make short term predictions seems very useful. GenAI is good at finding patterns.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, GenAI is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

One of the challenges that they face, after a day of seeing patients they need to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors.

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be a very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look a bigger than just an emergency room. In short look, it would seem we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problems, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^1]: Bank of Canada, [Time to Break the Glass: Fixing Canada's Productivity Problem](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/)
[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)
[^3]: Humber River Hospital Foundation, [Humber River Hospital's Command Centre Has Created 23 Virtual Beds](https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/)
[^4]: GE Healthcare, [Humber River Hospital Command Centre: One Year in Review](https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf) (PDF)

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove.{>>Claude: The reference only lands if the reader knows the film. One clause tying it back - a manufactured gap invented to justify a panic - would connect it to the 12%-to-60% adoption target.<<} Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive{--,--} doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why those sectors? {~~Based on what evidence.~>Based on what evidence?~~}{>>Claude: This section reads like margin notes and shows less rigour than the Healthcare deep-dive that follows. Either build one sector into a tight example or compress the whole thing to a couple of sentences and get to Healthcare faster.<<}

1. Health - improve Health Outcomes with AI? Where would we use AI and what evidence is there to support that it helps?
2. Energy and Natural Resources: AI used to optimize extraction and accelerate clean energy transformation? How
3. Transportation ...{>>Claude: Unfinished - this trails off. Give it the same one-line challenge as Health and Energy, or cut it.<<}

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy is too vague to be useful here.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector. In Ontario, we constantly hear stories of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.{>>Claude: Slight whiplash with "doesn't help" just before it. Tighten to one claim: it helps a handful leave faster but doesn't move the system.<<}

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that they there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. In this context, using an AI to find patterns and help make short term predictions seems very useful. GenAI is good at finding patterns.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, GenAI is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

One of the challenges that they face, after a day of seeing patients they need to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors.

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be a very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look a bigger than just an emergency room. In short look, it would seem we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problems, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove.{>>Claude: The reference only lands if the reader knows the film. One clause tying it back - a manufactured gap invented to justify a panic - would connect it to the 12%-to-60% adoption target.<<} Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive{--,--} doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why those sectors? {~~Based on what evidence.~>Based on what evidence?~~}{>>Claude: This section reads like margin notes and shows less rigour than the Healthcare deep-dive that follows. Either build one sector into a tight example or compress the whole thing to a couple of sentences and get to Healthcare faster.<<}

1. Health - improve Health Outcomes with AI? Where would we use AI and what evidence is there to support that it helps?
2. Energy and Natural Resources: AI used to optimize extraction and accelerate clean energy transformation? How
3. Transportation ...{>>Claude: Unfinished - this trails off. Give it the same one-line challenge as Health and Energy, or cut it.<<}

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy is too vague to be useful here.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector. In Ontario, we constantly hear stories of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.{>>Claude: Slight whiplash with "doesn't help" just before it. Tighten to one claim: it helps a handful leave faster but doesn't move the system.<<}

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that {~~they there is~>there is~~} enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. In this context, using an AI to find patterns and help make short term predictions seems very useful. GenAI is good at finding patterns.{>>Claude: Content check - a command centre doing bed forecasting and short-term operational predictions is almost certainly classical predictive analytics / ML, not GenAI. Labelling it GenAI here cuts against your own thesis that GenAI isn't the hero. Consider "the analytics" or "pattern-finding ML" and keep GenAI out of this example. (Same conflation in "using an AI to find patterns" just above.)<<}

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, GenAI is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

One of the challenges that they face, after a day of seeing patients they need to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions.{>>Claude: Run-on - two clauses stacked without a clean join. Try: "One challenge: after a day of seeing patients, they still have to write up charts documenting findings, treatment and prescriptions."<<} This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors.

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be a very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look a bigger than just an emergency room. In short look, it would seem we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problems, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove.{>>Claude: The reference only lands if the reader knows the film. One clause tying it back - a manufactured gap invented to justify a panic - would connect it to the 12%-to-60% adoption target.<<} Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive{--,--} doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why those sectors? {~~Based on what evidence.~>Based on what evidence?~~}{>>Claude: This section reads like margin notes and shows less rigour than the Healthcare deep-dive that follows. Either build one sector into a tight example or compress the whole thing to a couple of sentences and get to Healthcare faster.<<}

1. Health - improve Health Outcomes with AI? Where would we use AI and what evidence is there to support that it helps?
2. Energy and Natural Resources: AI used to optimize extraction and accelerate clean energy transformation? How
3. Transportation ...{>>Claude: Unfinished - this trails off. Give it the same one-line challenge as Health and Energy, or cut it.<<}

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy is too vague to be useful here.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector. In Ontario, we constantly hear stories of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. So speeding triage might help a few people leave emergency faster but it doesn't make a meaningful difference.{>>Claude: Slight whiplash with "doesn't help" just before it. Tighten to one claim: it helps a handful leave faster but doesn't move the system.<<}

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that {~~they there is~>there is~~} enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. In this context, using an AI to find patterns and help make short term predictions seems very useful. GenAI is good at finding patterns.{>>Claude: Content check - a command centre doing bed forecasting and short-term operational predictions is almost certainly classical predictive analytics / ML, not GenAI. Labelling it GenAI here cuts against your own thesis that GenAI isn't the hero. Consider "the analytics" or "pattern-finding ML" and keep GenAI out of this example. (Same conflation in "using an AI to find patterns" just above.)<<}

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, GenAI is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

One of the challenges that they face, after a day of seeing patients they need to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions.{>>Claude: Run-on - two clauses stacked without a clean join. Try: "One challenge: after a day of seeing patients, they still have to write up charts documenting findings, treatment and prescriptions."<<} This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors.{>>Claude: This sits in tension with the "documented problems" sentence just before. A half-clause reconciling them (they double-check the output? small sample of doctors?) keeps a skeptical reader from calling it a contradiction.<<}

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can {~~be a very useful.~>be very useful.~~} Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to {~~look a bigger than just~>look wider than just~~} an emergency room. {~~In short look, it would seem we want~>In short, we want~~} to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problems, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

**~15 marks: 7 comments (the judgement calls), 8 clean substitutions/cuts.**

Nothing on tone or off-voice vocabulary. The voice is solidly yours throughout, and the healthcare argument is the strong spine of the piece.

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why these sectors: Healthcare, Energy and Natural Resources, Transportation, Agriculture and Manufacturing.? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help.  it helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive, without making big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^1]: Bank of Canada, [Time to Break the Glass: Fixing Canada's Productivity Problem](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/)
[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)
[^3]: Humber River Hospital Foundation, [Humber River Hospital's Command Centre Has Created 23 Virtual Beds](https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/)
[^4]: GE Healthcare, [Humber River Hospital Command Centre: One Year in Review](https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf) (PDF)

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names all sorts of sectors where AI will create: "outsized value..." - why these sectors: Healthcare, Energy and Natural Resources, Transportation, Agriculture and Manufacturing.? Based on what evidence?

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help.  it helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI, however the AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can't see.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective, Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive, without making big difference. 

GenAI might help here, however we've solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn't a magic wand and it isn't a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can be a disaster.

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. "Increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports."[^2] I'm reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. 

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because {~~we hear about most often~>it's the one we hear about most often~~}. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn't make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we've sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help.{~~  it~> It~~} helps a handful leave faster but doesn't make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. 

Putting on our Systems Thinking hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go - walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system. 

One example of {~~hospital~>a hospital~~} taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they're paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

GE promotes this system as using AI{~~, however the~>. However, the~~} AI isn't the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they've studied the flow of the system. They've established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here's the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it "AI" but it's not the AI the strategy is betting on.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective{~~, Predictive~>. Predictive~~} analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity. 

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don't cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) When your business struggles financially, it's no surprise that doing charts is seen as an added burden.

Many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time with few, if any, errors. Possibly another example of GenAI making us feel more productive, without making big difference.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can't keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can't expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for a long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds. 

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement.
